data.title: Jensen Huang was also once an "Ethereum KOL".
data.description:
Author: Eric, Foresight News

In 2017, the cryptocurrency market was experiencing a booming bull run.

Jensen Huang, who has been dominating headlines worldwide in recent days, stated during Nvidia's earnings call that year, "Cryptocurrencies and blockchain will exist for a long time, and they will become very large... GPUs are well-positioned in this regard."

According to Nvidia's annual financial reports, it wasn't until 2023 that the revenue from data centers in Nvidia's chip business surpassed that from gaming for the first time.

Prior to this, gaming graphics cards and professional visualization tools were Nvidia's main businesses, but in those years, Ethereum mining, which accounted for a small percentage of its business, repeatedly disrupted Nvidia's stock price. The Ethereum bear market caused Nvidia to lose $20 billion in value. In March 2018, Jensen Huang had just celebrated his 55th birthday. In an interview with CNBC's "Mad Money," he reiterated what he had said in the previous year's earnings call: "Cryptocurrency will exist. The world will have a low-friction, low-cost way of exchanging value, and this way will exist for a long time." He also stated, "Blockchain will exist for a long time; it will become a completely new form of fundamental computing. I expect blockchain and cryptocurrency to be a major driver of GPU development." During those two years, JPMorgan Chase's CEO publicly called Bitcoin a fraud and said he would fire employees who traded Bitcoin; Buffett also repeatedly stated that cryptocurrencies would have a "bad ending"; AMD benefited more or less from its mining business, but very cautiously stated that "mining will not be a long-term growth driver." In today's terms, Jensen Huang would be considered a "mini-Musk." In 2016 and 2017, thanks to the rapid growth of its gaming and data center businesses, Nvidia's stock price rose by 224% and 81% respectively. But just as Huang was basking in the anticipation of further surprises from cryptocurrencies, a shock arrived first. In 2018, cryptocurrency prices collapsed across the board, with Bitcoin falling from nearly $20,000 to less than $4,000, and Ethereum even dropping from four figures back to double digits. In August 2018, Nvidia released its interim financial report, showing that revenue from crypto-related products plummeted from $289 million in the previous quarter to only $18 million. The company explicitly stated that crypto's contribution in the second half of the year would be negligible, and Nvidia's stock price fell by about 5% in after-hours trading. In November of the same year, Nvidia released its Q3 financial report, with revenue falling short of expectations. More importantly, it provided significantly lower guidance for the next quarter than Wall Street anticipated (approximately $2.7 billion vs. an expected $3.4 billion). During the conference call, Jensen Huang explicitly attributed the cause to a longer and more severe "crypto hangover" than expected. The following trading day after the report's release, Nvidia's stock price fell by as much as 19% from the previous day's closing price. A mining business that accounted for only a single-digit percentage of total revenue caused Nvidia's market capitalization to evaporate by over $20 billion in a single day. From "becoming a thing of the past" to "dedicated mining machines," in March 2019, at a press conference in Tel Aviv, Israel, Jensen Huang attempted to completely distance himself from cryptocurrencies. He told the media that Nvidia "never made any plans for cryptocurrencies. Cryptocurrencies found us, and they are a thing of the past." He acknowledged that crypto technology has its own value to some extent, and even hoped that the future blockchain world would find algorithms with lower computational intensity, so that GPUs would no longer be the battleground for miners. Clearly, Nvidia was badly hurt by the aggressive approach of cryptocurrency mining. But just two years later, things took a turn for the better. Starting in the second half of 2020, Ethereum prices soared, and Nvidia's gaming graphics cards once again became a hot commodity in the eyes of miners. RTX 30 series cards were in high demand and short supply, and gamers complained of being squeezed out of the market. News of internet cafes being completely booked for mining was commonplace. However, due to the previous bear market, miners struggled to find stable supply channels, leading to soaring retail prices and persistent shortages on e-commerce platforms. Gamers either had no graphics cards to use or bought "mining cards" that had already been completely sold out. Social media was abuzz with anger towards Nvidia. Jensen Huang realized that simply pretending cryptocurrencies didn't exist wouldn't solve the problem. In February 2021, Nvidia officially launched the Cryptocurrency Mining Processor, or CMP series. This was a device designed specifically for professional mining, with no display output, optimized for airflow, and supporting high-density multi-GPU deployments. This might not have been a reconciliation between Huang and cryptocurrencies, but rather a desire to avoid impacting core business. Evidence of this was Nvidia's implementation of driver-level limitations on the RTX 3060, roughly halving its Ethereum mining hashrate through the LHR mechanism, attempting to physically separate gamers and miners into two separate channels. Back then, a single order from Huang could send shivers down the spines of the Ethereum mining community. Although Bitmain also had Ethereum mining rigs at the time, and AMD graphics cards were even more efficient at mining, Nvidia's machines were always the first choice in terms of supply and product stability. The market initially reacted enthusiastically to CMP. In the first quarter of fiscal year 2021, CMP revenue exceeded $155 million. Nvidia optimistically predicted that it could reach $400 million in the next quarter, but the actual situation did not fully live up to this ambition; the actual revenue in the second quarter was approximately $266 million. By the third quarter, this figure had dropped to $105 million. Cumulatively, CMP brought Nvidia approximately $526 million in revenue throughout the cycle; Canadian mining company Hut8 once placed an order for $30 million worth of CMP equipment from Nvidia. Later, Nvidia even launched the higher-end CMP 170HX, with an Ethereum hashrate of approximately 164 MH/s and a price exceeding $4,000. However, its supply was quite limited, making it more of an experimental product for top-tier mining farms. With the launch of dedicated mining rigs, Jensen Huang's attitude towards cryptocurrencies underwent another 180-degree shift. In an interview with VentureBeat during Computex 2021, when asked if he was excited about Ethereum's transition to Proof-of-Stake (PoS), he gave an affirmative answer. In his view, Ethereum has established its position, possessing reliability and credibility, and many applications such as DeFi rely on its network to operate, making the transition to PoS a natural upgrade. He believes Ethereum has high long-term value, transaction processing speed is expected to improve significantly, and he made no secret of the fact that cryptocurrencies will continue to exist. He also stated that while the current hype surrounding Ethereum might cool down in a year, crypto mining itself will not disappear. Furthermore, he believes Ethereum chose GPUs because GPUs constitute the world's largest programmable distributed supercomputer network. In September 2022, the Ethereum merger, which excited Huang Renxun, was completed, and the demand for GPU mining collapsed overnight. Global mining farms shut down due to power outages, and a massive influx of used graphics cards flooded the market, instantly reversing the previous shortage to inventory backlog. Nvidia's CFO had to admit in subsequent financial reports that the Ethereum merger had negatively impacted demand for some products. However, starting in 2022, data center business gradually became Nvidia's core business, and the discontinuation of mining products did not have a significant impact on Nvidia. It was after this that Nvidia officially parted ways with cryptocurrencies. AI and Crypto If Huang Renxun hadn't run into trouble, we might have seen a third reversal in the future. Payments based on x402 and stablecoins are recognized as the best current solution for agent payments, and "AI+Crypto" projects have also secured a place in the current Web3 market. In March of this year, at the NVIDIA GTC 2026 conference, when Chamath Palihapitiya, host of the All-In Podcast, asked Jensen Huang for his opinion on Bittensor's training of low-parameter, large models using distributed computing power, Huang stated that it was a modern version of "Folding@home," and that open-source/decentralized models and closed-source models are complementary, like "A and B." Huang's endorsement caused the TAO token to surge by over 20% in a short period, with many on X expressing surprise that Huang himself had inadvertently endorsed a crypto project. With the continued development of AI, stablecoins or other cryptocurrencies may indeed become the currency for transactions between agents in the silicon-based era. Jensen Huang, who could have continued to discuss this extensively, will most likely not be the CEO of Nvidia, and will not be on a stage built by Nvidia, even if he has the opportunity to talk about this topic again in the future.

data.title: Anthropic calculates its market size using the wages of workers worldwide.
data.description:
On November 10, 2026, an AI company submitted an updated IPO prospectus. A prominent statement in the prospectus summary reads: "The work done by knowledge workers worldwide represents over $40 trillion in economic value in 2025." "Economic value" sounds like GDP, something abstract and grand. But this figure is followed by a small footnote 2. Turning to the methodology section, the first sentence states: "Several estimates in this prospectus regarding the wages of global knowledge workers are referred to as the annual economic value represented by global knowledge workers." The same figure, called "wages" in the footnote, is renamed "economic value" in the main text. This article's title doesn't invent anything; it simply changes the name. Other companies calculate the market by counting customers' software budgets; this company calculates the market by counting customers' payrolls. It's important to clarify that the prospectus does not use the term "market size." It calls wages "economic value," and then "the opportunity before us." Our interpretation is that it represents the market ceiling. But this interpretation isn't far-fetched. A software company willing to use total wages to measure its opportunity demonstrates what it's selling: not a better tool, but a portion of the labor that would otherwise be paid to people. According to a public report on November 10, 2026, the company planned to price its stock on November 18th (Eastern Time) and begin trading on November 19th. The market will assign it a price on that day. But this article doesn't intend to discuss the price. We want to follow that footnote a step further: if a large portion of this $40 trillion wage pool is indeed eaten up by the model, where will those people on the payroll go? This isn't a question about a particular stock. It's about you, your colleagues, and your child's first job ten years from now.

I. The bottom rungs of the ladder have loosened first

You may have noticed some inexplicable changes. There are fewer interns in the department. The words "recent graduate" appear less frequently in job postings. Tasks that used to be given to newcomers for practice, such as organizing spreadsheets, writing drafts, taking meeting minutes, and running tests, are increasingly being taken over by a dialog box. No one has been laid off. It's just that some people were never hired.

The person who spoke the loudest

In May 2025, the company's CEO said in a public interview: AI "may" eliminate half of the entry-level white-collar jobs within 1 to 5 years. This statement has been repeatedly quoted since then. It is not supported by a quantitative model; the original text used "could." It did not appear in the prospectus. But it came from the mouth of someone most qualified to know what the model can do. This gives its weight not from evidence, but from the person who spoke it.

The least sensitive data: Interestingly, the same company's economic research team released a labor market report in March 2026, which was later revised. They compared "occupations highly exposed to AI" with other occupations. The conclusion was restrained: the overall unemployment rate for high-exposure occupations did not show a systemic increase. The only signal came from young people. The entry rate for 22- to 25-year-olds into high-exposure occupations was about 14% lower than in 2022. There was no such decline among older groups. The authors themselves said that this result was only "barely significant." They also offered other explanations: young people who were not hired might have stayed in their original positions, changed careers, or returned to school. Another independent study using large-scale payroll records saw the same trend: employment for young people in high-exposure positions was relatively weaker, while employment for senior employees remained relatively stable.

How far can we go?

Putting all this together, we can only say that some studies suggest the door to white-collar jobs for young people is narrowing. We cannot say that AI has already caused large-scale unemployment. This is not yet visible in macro data. Mainstream estimates from international organizations also suggest that many jobs are exposed to AI, but exposure does not equal replacement; a significant portion will improve efficiency due to AI, rather than disappear. Therefore, the evidence here is "early, localized, and consistent." It's not an alarm, but a yellow light that has just been lit.

Layoffs will be in the news, but those not hired won't be. Replacement often occurs first in the blank spaces of statistical tables.

Why is it at the very bottom of the ladder?

One possible explanation is that the model excels at precisely the tasks newcomers use to practice. The value of experienced employees lies in judgment, relationships, and experience with complex situations. These are things the model cannot currently handle.

The value of new employees lies in completing standardized tasks and gradually growing into senior staff. If the model takes over this work, the company doesn't lose out in the short term: experienced employees become more efficient, and fewer new employees need to be hired. However, in the long run, a problem arises: if no one starts climbing from the bottom, where will the senior employees come from ten years from now? The prospectus itself addresses this issue. The risk factors list: the company's public statements regarding job replacement could be used against it in litigation or public disputes; if the public believes the model causes unemployment, it could trigger organized opposition; the government might intervene or slow down the adoption of AI to delay unemployment. The same payslip is described as "potentially disappearing jobs" in the CEO's interview, "expandable value" in the prospectus, and "potential trouble" in the risk factors. All three statements come from the same company. None of them are wrong.

II. Machines Take Away Many Jobs, But What Happened Afterwards

If you think this is unprecedented, history will first pour cold water on your view. This isn't the first time machines have taken jobs from human society. Each time, someone predicted mass unemployment; each time, the outcome was more complex than the prediction.

Those Who Smash Machines

In the early 19th century, textile workers in central England began smashing looms at night. They were later called Luddites. In later contexts, "Luddite" almost became synonymous with "opposition to progress." But this label is unfair. What those workers opposed wasn't entirely the machines themselves, but the way the machines arrived: skilled crafts became worthless within a few years, factory owners took the benefits of increased efficiency, and workers received lower wages and longer working hours.

In the long run, textile machines made clothing affordable for ordinary people, and industrialization ultimately raised the standard of living of the entire society to previously unimaginable heights. But the word "long run" was meaningless to the weavers at that time.

Economic historians generally note that in the early stages of the Industrial Revolution, for a considerable period, output grew rapidly, but the real wages of ordinary workers almost stagnated. The dividends were real. It just flowed into the factory owners' books first, and took a long time before reaching the workers' bowls. Machines never just take away jobs; they also determine who receives the dividends first. The second story is a bit more somber. After the widespread adoption of automobiles, horse-drawn carriages in cities disappeared almost within a generation. Coachmen, stable hands, and horseshoe makers—these professions shrank dramatically. Most people later found new jobs: drivers, mechanics, gas station employees, road builders. The number of jobs created by automobiles ultimately far exceeded the number eliminated. Horses were not so lucky. Their numbers declined steadily after the widespread adoption of automobiles and never returned. This is because horses could only provide one thing—physical strength—while the engine completely outperformed them in this regard. This comparison is often used to raise an uncomfortable question: In the face of general intelligence, are workers more like the coachmen of yesteryear, or more like the horses? Coachmen could switch professions because they had other skills to sell besides driving. Horses couldn't because they only had one skill, and that skill was completely replaced. Counter-argument: Bank tellers didn't disappear. But history doesn't always side with pessimists. When ATMs became widespread in the 1970s, many people thought bank tellers would disappear. After all, the teller's main tasks—depositing, withdrawing, and counting money—could all be done by machines. The reality was quite the opposite. In the decades following the widespread adoption of ATMs in the United States, the total number of bank tellers actually increased. The reason was that ATMs reduced the cost of opening a branch, so banks opened more branches. Each branch needed fewer tellers, but the total number of branches increased. The teller's job also changed, from counting money to financial advice, customer relations, and handling complex transactions. This is a classic case of "tool enhancement leading to job creation." It reminds us that a technology replacing a task in a job doesn't mean it will eliminate that job. ATMs didn't eliminate tellers; they eliminated the teller's original job content. History doesn't provide answers, it provides questions. Putting these stories together, we can roughly draw two conclusions. First, technology replaces tasks, not the entire job. When a job is broken down, some tasks are handed over to machines, while the remaining tasks may become more valuable or no longer require dedicated personnel. The outcome depends on the size of the remaining part. Second, after productivity increases, who benefits first is never determined by technology itself. In the early stages of the Industrial Revolution, it mainly flowed to capital; later, with the emergence of labor unions, labor legislation, public education, and social insurance, wages gradually caught up with productivity. In other words, the past technological waves ultimately led to widespread prosperity not because technology is inherently benevolent, but because society spent decades building a system to distribute the benefits. III. If This Time Is Truly Different So, what are the differences between this time and the past? It's not hands that are being replaced, it's the brain. In the past, machines mostly replaced physical labor and repetitive tasks. Looms replaced the weaver's hands, engines replaced the horse's legs, and ATMs replaced the teller's counting of money. Those who were replaced could often turn to things machines couldn't do: things requiring judgment, communication, and understanding complex situations. These tasks share a common name: cognitive labor. For the past two centuries, cognitive labor has been humanity's "refuge." With physical labor taken over by machines, people moved into office buildings. This time, the model is precisely targeting office buildings. Writing emails, reading contracts, creating reports, writing code, conducting research, and taking meeting minutes—these tasks were once considered "things machines couldn't do, so humans could always do them." By 2026, these are becoming the parts that models excel at. In the past, machines replaced hands; this time, it's the brain that's being repriced. From "Tool" to "Colleague" Another change lies hidden in the product's positioning. In industry parlance, models are increasingly less described as "a useful software" and more as a virtual collaborator: you give it a task, it breaks it down, executes it, checks it, and finally delivers a result. On November 10, 2026, the same day the company launched its roadshow, it released office products such as meetings, spreadsheets, and whiteboards. Its story extends from helping programmers write code to encompassing the daily work of almost all white-collar workers. The difference between a tool and a colleague lies in who gets paid. A good hammer makes a carpenter more valuable. A "colleague" who doesn't receive a salary, doesn't take vacations, and can simultaneously operate a hundred clones will make companies rethink: how many people are needed for this position? This is why it can measure its opportunities using total salary. What it sells can be understood as priced according to "how much workload is replaced"—this is an inference in this article, not a conclusion in the prospectus.

The Accounts of a Small Accounting Firm

Imagine a small accounting firm. In the past, it hired two fresh graduates every autumn. The newcomers started with voucher entry and reconciliation, working for two or three years to learn to understand a company's accounts before gradually taking on clients. One year, the partners discovered that a model could make voucher entry and reconciliation faster and more accurate, requiring only spot checks from senior accountants. That year, the firm only hired one person. The following year, none were hired. No one was fired. The senior accountants became busier and more valuable, and the firm's profits looked better.

But three years later, when a senior accountant retired, the partner realized: no one had ever worked their way up from the bottom using vouchers. The only replacement was either poached from another firm or they had to wait. This scenario is fictional, but every step of it makes sense in many industries. Over 11,900 corporate clients are already voting with their money. They aren't necessarily laying off employees; they're more likely hiring fewer people and having the same people do more work. But every such transaction ultimately ends up on the payroll. Where Will the 40 Trillion Go? Here's an easily overlooked detail: if models truly replace some cognitive labor, that portion of the wages won't disappear. It will go somewhere else. Part of it will remain with the client at a lower price. Companies use models to replace manual labor because it's cheaper, and most of the money saved won't go entirely to the model company. Part of it will become the model company's revenue, and then its shareholders' returns. Another portion may never reach anyone, because technological competition will continue to drive down prices, ultimately distributing the money among all consumers as cheaper goods and services. So, 40 trillion isn't a number that "will be eaten up," but rather a number that "will be moved." It originates from paychecks, flows to customers' profit statements, model companies' reports, and consumers' wallets. The problem lies in the proportion. If this money primarily flows to consumers, then it's a technological advancement similar to the past: things are cheaper, and everyone benefits. If it primarily flows to shareholders of a few companies, then we are facing an unprecedented redistribution of wealth. 40 trillion isn't money that disappears; it's money that changes hands: from paychecks to shareholder lists. It's also possible that this time won't be different. To be fair, we must seriously consider another possibility: this time, perhaps it won't be so different. The first reason is history itself. Every time a technological wave arrives, the claim that "this time will be different" emerges, and most of the time, it has proven wrong. Human society's ability to create new jobs has repeatedly exceeded the imagination of its contemporaries. At the beginning of this century, no one could have predicted that "content creator," "data labeler," and "user growth manager" would become professions for tens of thousands of people. We can't imagine what new professions will emerge ten years from now. The second reason is the difference between a task and a job. A position often consists of dozens of tasks. A model that can do some of them doesn't mean it can take over the entire position. Lawyers don't just read contracts; they also assess their clients' situations, negotiate with the opposing party, and persuade judges in court. Doctors don't just read X-rays; they also talk to patients and take responsibility. A rather conservative academic estimate suggests that in the next ten years, AI will only cost-effectively replace a small portion of all tasks. Its exposure is broad, but its replacement is narrow. The third reason is the speed of implementation. When a company adopts a new technology, it needs to change processes, organization, and performance evaluations, and also deal with regulatory and legal risks. It took decades for electricity to go from invention to truly improving factory productivity. The popularization of models may be much faster, but it will still have to overcome these frictions. The fourth and most compelling reason is that these jobs are more likely to transform than disappear. Just like tellers in the ATM era, the job responsibilities of accountants, programmers, and analysts may be rewritten: less repetitive work and more judgment, communication, and monitoring models. According to this view, the decline in hiring rates may simply be the growing pains of a transitional period: companies haven't figured out what new employees should do, so they're hiring less initially. Once the new job structures take shape, the doors will reopen. These reasons are not mere speculation. They have historical support, and a significant number of scholars agree with them. We cannot prove them wrong. We can only say that if they are correct, then the best outcome is "transformation"; even with transformation, who will bear the costs during the transition period remains a question that needs to be answered.

A review of the top ten potential candidates in the market, which may directly affect whether you can buy the dip.

Jensen Huang, the soul of Nvidia for 33 years and co-founder, has suddenly left in a way that neither Silicon Valley nor Wall Street expected.

Affected by recent extramarital affair scandals and potential national security compliance investigations, Nvidia officially announced on Thursday (November 12) that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately. To stabilize the situation, Nvidia's board of directors quickly appointed Colette Kress, the CFO who has served the company for 13 years, as interim CEO (while retaining the CFO position; since Kress has no engineering background, she is generally regarded as a transitional option), and hired top external headhunting firms to fully launch the selection process for a formal successor.

Who will ultimately take over the "leather jacket" symbolizing global AI computing power dominance? This is undoubtedly one of the most concerning topics in the market right now.

This morning, US President Trump publicly called on social media to nominate former Apple CEO and current Executive Chairman Tim Cook to lead the company. Meanwhile, financial media outlets such as Bloomberg are actively compiling a list of candidates from within the company, chip industry peers, and cloud giants. On the prediction market Polymarket, the number of potential successors to Jensen Huang has increased to 24. This article will use prediction market probabilities as a benchmark to list the top ten most likely candidates to succeed Jensen Huang and analyze the potential advantages and disadvantages of choosing internal promotion or external appointment. Top Ten Potential Candidates: A Comprehensive Overview Based on industry analysis from various media outlets and the latest odds data from the market, Nvidia's leadership search has been divided into three camps: internal core veterans, external semiconductor giants, and "legendary wildcards" handpicked by political and business figures. Internal Promotion Channels: The First Choice for Stabilizing the Core Team Because Jensen Huang has long implemented a flat management structure without a deputy at the group level, Nvidia has formed a multi-sector structure encompassing software, finance, networking, sales, and cutting-edge research. The heads of these different sectors are all considered top candidates. Ian Buck – Vice President of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, NVIDIA Polymarket win rate (as of 10:20 AM Beijing time, November 13): 30%, currently the top favorite. Core strengths: Widely recognized as the "Father of CUDA." He has worked at NVIDIA for over 20 years, spearheading the software revolution that transformed GPUs from graphics cards into general-purpose parallel computing platforms, and is a key driver in NVIDIA's data center business growing from nothing to a multi-billion dollar scale. Succession rationale: NVIDIA's true moat is not only its chips, but also its deeply integrated hardware and software CUDA ecosystem. Buck has an intimate understanding of the company's technology roadmap (from Blackwell to the subsequent Rubin architecture), and his succession will best reassure the internal R&D team and core cloud vendor customers. Colette Kress – NVIDIA Interim CEO and CFO Polymarket Win Rate: 17%, currently ranked second Core Strengths: Recruited personally by Jensen Huang in 2013 with an AI blueprint drawn on a whiteboard. Prior to that, she has nearly 25 years of finance and operations experience at Microsoft (former CFO of the Server and Tools division), Cisco, and Texas Instruments. During her tenure, she led NVIDIA to achieve over 50-fold annual revenue growth and is NVIDIA's most familiar and trusted "financial megaphone" on Wall Street. Succession Rationale: At a time when the founder's personal scandal has triggered a corporate governance crisis, and the company faces a sensitive period marked by a $164.5 billion financial commitment to data centers and the US-China chip export control dispute, Kress possesses extremely high credibility in the capital markets, making him the safest bet for a smooth transition. Michael Kagan – Nvidia Chief Technology Officer (CTO) Polymarket Winning Rate: 4% Core Strengths: A top Israeli computer architect who worked at Intel for 16 years (leading the Pentium MMX architecture), co-founded the high-speed networking giant Mellanox in 1999 and served as its CTO for over 20 years. Following Nvidia's $7 billion acquisition of Mellanox in 2020, Kagan became Nvidia's CTO, overseeing Nvidia's largest R&D base outside the United States (the Israel R&D Center). The rationale for his appointment: The bottleneck of the Wanka AI cluster has long since shifted from "single-card computing power" to "high-speed interconnect" (InfiniBand and NVLink). Kagan is the chief architect who defines the modern data center as "a giant computer" (AI factory), and his succession aligns perfectly with Nvidia's technological strategy of transforming into a full-stack system provider. Jay Puri – Former Executive Vice President of Global Business Operations, NVIDIA, now Senior Advisor. Polymarket Win Rate: 3%. Core Strengths: NVIDIA's second-longest-serving executive and head of monetization. He holds a Master's degree in Electrical Engineering from Caltech and an MBA from Harvard Business School. After 22 years at Sun Microsystems, he joined NVIDIA in 2005, leading global sales, key account relations, and regional markets for 21 years. Succession Rationale: He is one of the few veterans in NVIDIA's senior management team with both a strong engineering background and global business development skills. He directly liaises with major global sovereign AI buyers and hyperscale cloud vendors, and is familiar with the business dynamics behind every multi-billion dollar order. However, Prie has recently stepped back from active management and transitioned to a senior advisory role this fall, reducing the likelihood of him being directly appointed CEO. Bill Dally – Chief Scientist and Senior Vice President of Research, NVIDIA [Image of a Polymarket win rate: 2%] Core Strengths: A leading figure in global computer architecture and former chair of the Computer Science Department at Stanford University. Since joining NVIDIA in 2009, he has single-handedly built NVIDIA Research, leading breakthroughs in almost all the underlying technologies that have laid the foundation for today's AI dominance, including Tensor Cores, NVLink high-speed interconnect, and low-precision inference. Succession Logic: As the company's "technical brain" and a member of the Presidential Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), Daly enjoys extremely high prestige in academia, politics, and engineering, and is a spiritual icon for maintaining Nvidia's technological edge over the next decade. External Parachuting Options: Top Tech Leaders in the Semiconductor World If the board decides to seek external assistance, the market predicts that the top picks will be highly concentrated on three executives from chip giants who understand hardware and architecture and can control TSMC's production capacity. Rene Haas – CEO of Arm Polymarket Win Rate: 12%, tied for first place among external candidates Core Advantages: Combines experience as a CEO of a listed company with the background of a former Nvidia executive. He served as Vice President and General Manager of NVIDIA's Computing Products Business Unit from 2006 to 2013, a tenure of seven years. After taking the helm at Arm, he successfully led the company through its IPO and its transformation into a data center and AI computing platform. The rationale for his appointment: He understands NVIDIA's unique internal culture and possesses global ecosystem resources for mobile and server CPU architectures (NVIDIA's Grace CPU is based on the Arm architecture), making him a rare candidate with both internal and external expertise. Johny Srouji – Chief Hardware Technology Officer (Senior Vice President) of Apple Inc. Polymarket Success Rate: 12%, tied for first place among external candidates. Core Strengths: Creator of Apple's self-developed chip empire (Apple Silicon, encompassing A-series and M-series chips), possessing unparalleled iron-fisted execution capabilities in advanced process architecture design, hardware-software synergy, and control over TSMC's core production capacity. Reasoning for Appointment: Nvidia is currently operating at an extreme R&D pace of "one iteration per year" and is heavily reliant on TSMC's advanced packaging and wafer capacity. Srouji's engineering prestige and supply chain control are highly compatible with Nvidia's hardware foundation needs.

Lisa Su – Chairwoman and CEO of AMD

Polymarket win rate: 4%

Core strengths: PhD in Electrical Engineering from MIT, a recognized "Iron Lady" in the semiconductor industry. After taking over the struggling AMD, she dealt a heavy blow to Intel in the data center market with her Zen architecture CPUs and launched the MI series AI accelerator cards, becoming the only competitor currently able to directly challenge Nvidia in the AI ​​computing power market.

Rationale for succession: From the perspective of pure technical depth, supply chain influence, and business acumen, Lisa Su is almost the only chip leader in the world who can be considered on par with Jensen Huang (and the two are also distant cousins). However, as the leader of the number one arch-rival, this option reflects more the market's projections and faces enormous practical obstacles.

The "Legendary Wildcard" Called for by Political and Business Circles: Former Giant Company LeadersHuang Renxun's resignation not only involves personal ethics but also Congressional and FBI scrutiny of potential national security risks. Therefore, two Silicon Valley godfathers with top-tier political and business acumen have entered the top ten in the odds. Tim Cook – Former CEO and current Executive Chairman of Apple Inc. Polymarket Winning Rate: 5% Core Advantage: Trump's Handpicked Successor – Following Jensen Huang's resignation, US President Trump publicly named him on social media on Thursday: "Now that the exceptionally successful Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned, only one person can take his place, and that is Tim Cook of Apple. One legend succeeds another." Succession Logic: Cook has proven at Apple how, after the departure of the legendary founder (Steve Jobs), he propelled a technology company to the pinnacle of a multi-trillion dollar market capitalization through exceptional global supply chain control, sound financial discipline, and the ability to lobby politically and business-wise between major powers. Eric Schmidt – Former CEO and Executive Chairman of Google Polymarket Winning Rate: 2% Core Strength: Silicon Valley's most renowned "adult supervision." He joined Google in 2001 as CEO and served for ten years, assisting the two young founders in transforming Google from a startup into a global internet giant. After stepping down, he was active in Washington's defense and AI policy circles (serving as chairman of the National Artificial Intelligence Security Council) and heavily invested in the AI ​​sector. Succession Logic: Some Wall Street analysts point out that Nvidia's biggest pain point is that the 60 direct subordinates left by Jensen Huang lack the prestige to handle political storms in Wall Street and Washington. Schmidt possesses expertise in large-scale AI strategy and deep connections within the Pentagon and the White House, making him an ideal transitional leader to help Nvidia quell the national security investigation storm. Internal Promotion vs. External Appointment: The Board's Weighing of Pros and Cons Nvidia is not a company that employs a conventional professional management system. Over the past 33 years, Jensen Huang has built an extremely unique organizational structure—a highly flat management structure, engineering agility based on "lightning speed," and a heavy coupling of hardware and software integration. This makes the selection of a leader a complex game. If "internal promotion" (such as by Buck, Kress, or Kagan) is chosen, its biggest advantages are "stability" and "speed." On one hand, there is a seamless alignment between the technology roadmap and customer expectations. Nvidia is currently at a critical juncture, ramping up production of the Blackwell architecture and rapidly developing the Rubin architecture. Internal core veterans do not need to spend months re-understanding the complex CUDA software stack and NVLink network architecture. Meanwhile, hyperscale cloud providers like Microsoft, Google, and Meta have long directly negotiated product roadmaps and multi-billion dollar orders with Buck, Prie, and Kress. Having insiders take over minimizes the wait-and-see attitude of major clients and the associated friction costs. On the other hand, it also protects Nvidia's unique engineering culture. External executives are often accustomed to the hierarchical and bureaucratic management processes of traditional tech giants; forcibly imposing such systems could easily undermine Nvidia's proud flat and agile decision-making structure. Internal veterans, however, are naturally suited to this high-intensity, engineering-oriented operating model, which can maximize the stability of the R&D team. However, the shortcomings of internal promotion are equally apparent. First, there's a lack of experience in managing a listed company's top executives. Whether it's Buck and Kagan, who focus on technology and business, or Kress, who focuses on finance, none of them had previously independently led a multinational tech empire worth nearly $4 trillion. They lack direct experience in dealing with complex geopolitical games, congressional national security reviews, and global antitrust regulations. Second, there's the challenge of balancing power among internal factions. Previously, Huang could manage 60 senior executives single-handedly thanks to his co-founder's absolute authority. Now, promoting someone from a senior vice president at the same level could easily disrupt the delicate internal power balance. Furthermore, facing the onslaught of cloud vendors' self-developed ASIC chips, those maintaining the status quo often fall into path dependency, lacking the courage to break out of the existing framework and disrupt the business model. Conversely, if an "external parachute" (including industry leaders or heads of other large companies) is chosen, the board values ​​"breaking the deadlock" and "reshaping." The core advantage lies first and foremost in mature corporate governance and crisis management capabilities. External leaders like Haas, Cook, and Schmidt have already proven their dominance in independently helming mega-corporations in the capital markets. Nvidia's leadership change stems from the founder's personal scandals and potential national security compliance crises. Bringing in an external CEO with a strong resume and outstanding reputation can not only quickly appease the shaken Wall Street institutional investors but also send a strong signal to the outside world that "corporate governance has been completely overhauled, no longer relying on the halo of a single founder." At the same time, cross-industry expertise is expected to fill Nvidia's gaps—bringing in Apple executives (Srugie or Cook) could push the control of chip design and TSMC's supply chain to its extreme; bringing in political and business magnates (Schmidt) or executives from cloud giants could quickly repair relations with Washington or accelerate the transformation into a full-stack cloud service provider. However, external appointments are also a high-stakes gamble with significant costs. The biggest hidden danger lies in the strong "cultural rejection reaction" and the loss of core talent. Nvidia's core technology team has an almost religious sense of identity with the company. If a new leader tries to implement sweeping organizational restructuring or introduce cumbersome KPI assessments, it is very likely to trigger a wave of resignations among core vice presidents and top chip architects. Even more fatal is the long strategic integration period—in the fast-paced AI computing power arms race, any strategic gap of six months to a year caused by a new leader becoming familiar with the business could give AMD and cloud vendors' self-developed ASIC camp an excellent breathing space and a window to counterattack.

The Real Difficulty of Poaching from Competitors

Although the market has given Haas (12%), Slugi (12%), Cook (5%), and Su Zifeng (4%) relatively high odds, in terms of business practice, directly poaching senior executives from competitors or core ecosystem partners faces three almost insurmountable real barriers. The first barrier is the trade secret lawsuit and the lengthy "garden leave." Although California law, where Nvidia is headquartered, does not generally support non-compete agreements, the federal and state Trade Secrets Protection Acts (DTSA/UTSA) still wield considerable power. Take Lisa Su or Slugie as examples: they possess the underlying architecture of AMD or Apple's chips for the next 3 to 5 years, TSMC's advanced process capacity lock-in agreements, and key customer pricing strategies. If they jump ship to a direct competitor or Nvidia, which is also vying for TSMC's capacity, their former employers will inevitably file lawsuits, invoking the "inevitable disclosure" doctrine—arguing that it was impossible for them not to use their former company's core trade secrets while working at Nvidia—and thus seeking a preliminary injunction to force them into a paid "garden leave" period of 1 to 2 years. In the rapidly evolving AI era, Nvidia cannot afford to wait for a new leader to be out of work for over a year before officially taking office. The second barrier comes from the iron fist of global antitrust agencies. Nvidia currently holds over 80% of the global market share in AI acceleration chips for data centers, and is already under the scrutiny of the US Department of Justice (DOJ), the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), and the European Commission's antitrust scrutiny. If the board attempts to poach Lisa Su from AMD, considering that AMD is Nvidia's only substantial counterweight in the GPU field, its top leader's move to Nvidia, while not a corporate acquisition, could easily be classified by regulators as "maliciously undermining market competition" or talent monopoly, thus attracting even stronger antitrust investigations and administrative intervention. And if they attempt to poach Haas from Arm, the historical resistance is equally formidable. From 2020 to 2022, Nvidia attempted to acquire Arm for $40 billion, but ultimately failed due to joint opposition from regulatory agencies in multiple countries and giants such as Qualcomm and Microsoft. The core issue was the regulatory requirement to ensure the "absolute neutrality" of the Arm architecture. If Arm's current CEO were to switch leadership to Nvidia now, chip giants like Apple, Qualcomm, and Broadcom, which also rely on the Arm instruction set, would inevitably put pressure on global regulators again, accusing the two companies of potential ecosystem bias and transfer of benefits. The third barrier is the exorbitant "golden handcuffs" and the protracted transaction negotiations. Whether it's Lisa Su, Haas, or Apple's Sruggie, they all hold hundreds of millions of dollars worth of unvested restricted stock (RSUs) and long-term performance stock (PSUs) in their original companies. If Nvidia wants to poach them, it not only needs its board to approve an unprecedentedly high "buyout compensation package"—which is likely to cause controversy among shareholders when the company has just experienced a scandal and a significant drop in market value; it also has to face various defensive retention measures and legal negotiations by the original board of directors, which will indefinitely prolong the entire negotiation and closing cycle. Whoever it is, they will have to redefine Nvidia without Jensen Huang. Looking at the odds distribution on Polymarket, traders who are willing to spend real money are clearly aware of the legal and antitrust obstacles to poaching from outside—among the top ten candidates, Nvidia's internal executives occupy half, and the combined success rate of just Barker (30%) and Kress (17%) is close to 50%. After Jensen Huang's sudden departure from the central leadership, Nvidia has effectively entered a delicate "dual-core transition period." Externally, interim CEO Kress will preside over next week's Q3 earnings call to reassure shaken Wall Street institutions and regulators; internally, it heavily relies on veteran technologists like Buck and Kagan to stabilize R&D and deliveries to major cloud providers. Regardless of whether an internal executive ultimately takes over or an external figure is parachuted in to resolve the situation, the new leader must answer the ultimate question: when that iconic leather jacket is absent, is Nvidia's nearly $4 trillion empire operating on individual heroism, or has it become a perfectly functioning, self-sustaining machine?

Author: insights4vc Source: Substack Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

AI is becoming a meaningful business interface, but it is still far from becoming a significant independent buyer. Consumers use AI to research products, compare alternatives, and then enter merchant websites with a clear purchase intention. Evidence suggesting that consumers have generally handed over spending decisions to AI is much weaker. However, recent data from China suggests that AI embedded in mature shopping apps can influence purchases long before independent agents become the primary transaction channel.

This distinction changes the investment problem itself. Opportunities depend on which transactions become cheaper, easier, or more reliable when coordinated by software, and which companies still retain control over distribution, licensing, and fulfillment.

Stablecoins are included in this analysis because agents need payment methods. They can streamline the purchase of digital services and some cross-border transfers, especially in scenarios where both parties already hold compatible assets. Agents can also spend money via bank cards, instant bank transfers, or corporate accounts. Changes in discovery, purchasing authorization, and settlement infrastructure each have their own economics and require their own evidence. E-commerce penetration has never been solely determined by technology. Quarterly data from the U.S. Census Bureau documents a process of gradual expansion and disruption by a single, unusual shock. The seasonally adjusted share of online retail rose from 0.6% in Q4 1999 to 2.2% in Q4 2004, 4.1% in Q4 2009, and 11.2% in Q4 2019. The average annual growth rate accelerated from 0.35 percentage points in the first decade to 0.71 percentage points in the second decade. The smartphone era coincided with even faster growth, but this overall timeline cannot separate the impact of smartphones from improvements in broadband, e-commerce platforms, payment processing, or delivery. Between the fourth quarter of 2019 and the second quarter of 2020, this percentage jumped 5.1 percentage points to 16.3%, before falling back to 14.6% in the fourth quarter of 2021. Forced changes in shopping habits and reduced offline spending both affected this rate. Data released in August 2026 showed a figure of 17.1% for the second quarter of 2026; the U.S. Census Bureau subsequently noted that a revised version was scheduled for release on November 19, later than the data cutoff date in this article.

These denominators make it impossible to determine the relative penetration rates between countries. Online shopping participation in Europe has increased by 16 percentage points over the past decade, but the 2025 results vary from 57% in Bulgaria to 95% in Ireland. China's published retail share data shows that its online physical goods channels are far greater than Japan's, while South Korea's figures describe the device choices within online businesses. China's revised statistical methods also require caution when constructing continuous growth sequences. This article does not establish comparable long-term purchase sequences for various sectors in emerging markets.

Observed traffic data shows that commercial value appears further down the funnel. In Adobe's September US retail analysis, AI-driven visitors had a 90% higher conversion rate and generated 83% more revenue per visit; the traffic itself grew by 71% year-over-year. The analysis covered over 1 trillion visits, 100 million products, and 18 categories. Those conversion figures are not from another survey of over 5,000 people.

Observed traffic data shows that commercial value appears further down the funnel.

... Under any billing model, agents still need an executable budget, an available list of suppliers, expiring authorizations, and auditable credentials. Which transactions are worth entrusting? The economic test is whether the savings in time, price, and coordination outweigh the losses from reasoning, integration, oversight, and anticipated errors. Repeat purchases make small savings valuable, but a familiar two-minute replenishment leaves less room for improvement than reconciling invoices across supplier portals. Corporate procurement already has established approval policies; agents must earn their place by handling exceptions or extending supplier coverage beyond existing automation. For households, narrow replenishment instructions can specify caps on goods, quantities, and prices. Group catering adds a coordination problem involving multiple preferences and a single budget. Complex travel offers greater potential savings, but the consequences of cancellations or mishandling of transit are also more costly. The strongest initial candidates are those scenarios that combine limited authorization with verifiable outcomes before losses accumulate. The Jane Street roundtable's emphasis on short feedback loops in the question of whether the AI ​​singularity is imminent suggests a more discerning test: what proves a purchase was successful, when that evidence arrives, and what remains to be revoked? A valid API response confirms delivery, not necessarily accuracy; a product identifier confirms variation, not fit or satisfaction. Our inference is that delegation becomes attractive only when verification costs and residual expected losses are lower than the reconciliation savings. Contracts that specify observable acceptance testing and remedies can expand this set. When outcomes are subjective or delayed, stronger model capabilities may still not eliminate the costly manual inspection. Value creation and value capture may be separate. Controlling product discovery is already a lucrative business. Amazon reported third-quarter advertising revenue of $19.637 billion, up 11% year-over-year, although that figure includes business beyond retail-sponsored merchandise. Reuters reported in November that Amazon and Walmart are testing ads in their respective shopping assistants. Amazon says agent shopping has not yet had a substantial impact on its advertising business. This could change as more purchasing decisions move to AI interfaces. A Wharton study in August 2026 provides early indications of how these decisions might be influenced. Researchers ran approximately 26,000 simulated fitness watch selections across six models and eight products. In another experiment involving four models, presenting three recommendation sources simultaneously shifted GPT-5.5 by 53 percentage points relative to the baseline towards Wircutter's product. Providing the same sources sequentially had almost no effect. The products themselves remained unchanged. These were simulated choices, not real purchases, but the results demonstrate that whoever controls the information reaching the assistant can potentially influence which merchants receive demand. Independent assistants can use aggregated purchase intent to negotiate better prices or commissions. Retailers can respond by embedding similar tools into their existing platforms, where they already control catalogs, customer relationships, and fulfillment. Standardized interfaces may diminish the value of basic product matching, but inventory, delivery networks, and reliable dispute resolution remain more difficult to replicate. For merchants, economics depend on whether the agent brings in genuine new customers. Imagine a 20% contribution margin and a 5% commission on all sales generated by agent referrals. If existing customers would have made a purchase without additional acquisition costs, then for more than 25% of referral sales to be incremental, the commission is worthwhile. Lower advertising spending improves this calculation, while returns, support costs, and customer data churn are detrimental. Looking solely at GMV generated by agents provides very limited insight into profitability. Customer relationships are more important than the first transaction. An assistant that retains purchase history and preferences can direct future orders to competing suppliers, potentially reducing a merchant's customer lifetime value. Open sourcing allows merchants to reach multiple assistants, limiting reliance on any single intermediary. Payment processors can still profit from credentials, fraud prevention, and verification, regardless of the settlement method. Stablecoin issuers benefit from balances, while wallet service providers and payment infrastructure companies need sufficient fee revenue to cover operating costs. Higher transaction volume does not automatically translate into higher retention revenue. Commission-based recommendations introduce another problem. Assistants might favor paying merchants, retain a portion of negotiated discounts, or direct orders to the highest bidder. These don't necessarily represent today's market, but each creates a potential conflict between the buyer's interests and the intermediary's revenue. Evaluating these models requires transparency regarding compensation, final transaction prices, and repeat purchase behavior. The issue isn't just how much business agents facilitate, but how much value they create and who ultimately takes it. **Conclusion** Agent commerce is progressing fastest where AI improves existing buying relationships. Embedded assistants can leverage existing catalogs, payment credentials, and fulfillment networks to influence discovery and conversion. Fully delegated purchasing introduces additional requirements: authorization to spend money, access to merchants, and confidence that the purchase fulfills the customer's instructions. Therefore, the growth of assistance provides opportunities for delegation, rather than a reliable measure of the degree of delegation adoption. The economic boundary lies in establishing the cost of "the agent doing the right thing." Bounded purchases with observable outcomes and available remedies provide the clearest starting point. When preferences are subjective, delivery delays are high, or errors are costly, validation and monitoring can devour the time saved. Improved model capabilities expand the viable market, while surrounding business controls determine how much of that capability becomes useful. The channel remains central to value capture. The shopping experiments reviewed in this paper show that product selection may depend on what information reaches the assistant and how it is presented. Control over these inputs, even when checkout agreements are open, can affect the demand received by merchants. Whether this effect generates sustainable profits depends on incremental sales, customer retention, and the ability of intermediaries to charge without eliminating the benefits for buyers or merchants. Stablecoins reinforce this proposition where supplier onboarding or settlement friction is reduced. Their economic viability still depends on funding, financing, acceptance, and relief, with traditional billing methods being competitive alternatives. The next phase should be judged by recurring usage, incremental contributions from merchants, and the total cost of each correctly completed purchase. Suppliers who make delegation measurable, economical, and traceable will have a stronger foundation for retaining revenue as adoption grows.
