data.title: How much is Nvidia worth without Jensen Huang?
data.description: Nvidia's stock price has been performing poorly for some time, especially during Jensen Huang's tenure as CEO. His sudden resignation gives investors a chance to reassess. Once all the negative news has been priced in, the investigations have concluded, and a new CEO is appointed as scheduled, Nvidia will return to chip manufacturing. And the world's demand for chips will be as high as it was last week. Nvidia's global dominance is largely attributed to its charismatic founder, Jensen Huang. No one can and should deny his influence on the astonishing rise of generative artificial intelligence. Large language models are changing the future of computing and the way we work and think. And the graphics processing units (GPUs) that Huang initially built for gaming remain at the heart of it all. On Thursday, Huang resigned as CEO amid allegations (partially admitted) surrounding an extramarital affair and national security concerns. "The Nvidia Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer, and member of the Board of Directors, effective immediately," the company said in a statement Thursday morning. This was a statement no one would have expected a month ago. But on Sunday night, November 8th, when Jensen Huang said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children," this outcome became increasingly likely. Nvidia's stock price subsequently plummeted, continuing its decline until Huang resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's latest closing price was $166, down 31% from its October peak. This self-inflicted crisis has given customers, Wall Street, and Nvidia itself an opportunity to reassess. Frankly, even with Huang in charge, Nvidia's stock has performed poorly recently. For over a year, investors have treated Nvidia as a value stock, paying little premium for its enormous growth prospects. Now, its valuation resembles that of a distressed asset. Changing CEOs is painful for everyone involved, but it's also an opportunity for the company to prove itself again. And the good news is, as Barron's has long argued, Nvidia's products are a "gold mine" in the tech world. “Nvidia remains one of the best stocks I’ve ever found and invested in,” said Bill Gundsen, a partner at GCG Advisory Partners. “Focus on earnings! Don’t look at Jensen Huang.” Its earnings remain substantial. According to FactSet, Nvidia is projected to earn over $200 billion in calendar year 2026, compared to less than $600 million in 2012—the year researchers at the University of Toronto used GPUs to train neural networks that beat traditional computers in a visual recognition challenge, a pivotal moment in the development of deep learning and AI. Over the past five years, its earnings have grown at an average annual rate of over 80%. Wall Street analysts predict it will maintain an average annual earnings growth of 40% over the next three years. Typically, such growth is accompanied by a high price-to-earnings ratio. Any conservative investor would be happy to accept a valuation multiple that matches the company’s earnings growth. But today, Nvidia’s stock price is less than 12 times its projected earnings for the next 12 months, close to the stock’s all-time low P/E ratio, and significantly discounted from the S&P 500’s P/E ratio of 18. Baird analyst Tristan Gerra downgraded Nvidia's stock rating from "Outperform" to "Neutral," becoming the first analyst this week to call for a change in CEO. He believes a fair price-to-earnings ratio of 13. He forecasts $20 per share for fiscal year 2028 (Nvidia's fiscal year ends in January). Based on this, the stock price would reach $260 in about a year, meaning even more cautious analysts believe there is still 60% upside potential from recent levels. If Nvidia can somehow return to its five-year average price-to-earnings ratio of nearly 30, the current stock could theoretically reach $450, an increase of approximately 160%. There are also signs that Nvidia's stock price is bottoming out. This week has seen the most active trading week for Nvidia stock since April 2025. Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies and a market technical analyst, says it feels like a “surrender sell-off.” She’s not judging Nvidia from a fundamental perspective. Technical analysts analyze investor behavior through candlestick patterns and historical data. Stockton believes the stock price has support around $164, with additional support around $150. This means a worst-case scenario of a further $20 drop, or 10%, downside. Upside potential is between 50% and 150%. In terms of risk-reward, Nvidia is a rare opportunity now. “I’ve been watching corporate dramas like Nvidia for 30 years,” says Gary Black, co-founder of One Global ETF. “Investors should buy on the day Jensen Huang resigns, when uncertainty is at its highest and portfolio managers are finally facing reality.” However, the outcome may not be so simple. Nvidia's story isn't just about profitability; its products and balance sheet have become the "connecting thread" of the entire AI deal. Moreover, the company is currently facing a leadership vacuum. CFO Colette Kress has taken over temporarily, but she is unlikely to be a long-term board member. Nvidia under Jensen Huang is known for its flat organizational structure, with dozens of employees reporting directly to him. This flat management structure may have fostered innovation, but it has also made it difficult for investors—and perhaps the company itself—to find a credible successor. "Jensen Huang is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. "That doesn't mean they can't find a Tim Cook in the future, but the company isn't prepared for it." Tim Cook has almost become synonymous with a leader who successfully succeeds a legendary founder in Silicon Valley. In the 15 years since Tim Cook took over as CEO from Steve Jobs, Apple stock has returned approximately 2700%. However, Nvidia's talent pool may not be as lacking as feared. Melius Research analyst Ben Reithis sees several potential internal candidates, including Ian Barker, VP in charge of hyperscale cloud business and the highly valuable CUDA programming platform that keeps customers using Nvidia chips; Jonah Alben, in charge of GPU engineering; Michael Kagan, CTO; Bill Daly, Chief Scientist; Deborah Shoquist, head of operations and supply chain; and Nick Park, executive vice president who has worked at Microsoft for over 26 years. Outside the company, many experienced managers would be vying to lead Nvidia. But none of them are Jensen Huang—a reality that the stock price has already fully (even excessively) reflected.

data.title: Technological Revolution and the “World Brain”: How the Telephone Reshapes an Era
data.description:
Author: James Gleick Source: a16z Frontier Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Editor's Note: When the telephone was first invented, people had many ideas about its uses. It could have been a better telegraph, a way to broadcast concerts, or a new gossip channel. What it would actually become was only clear a long time later.

In his new book, *The Telephone: A New History*, James Gleick—author of *Chaos: The New Science* and biographies of Newton and Feynman—goes back to an era when what we now take for granted was still an open question. The inventor had his own plans, and the users had other intentions.

With the publisher's permission, we share an excerpt from this new book, because we keep returning to the question: once a new technology is available, what do people do with it?

The last few decades of the nineteenth century are now considered the Second Industrial Revolution. Some historians go even further: Václav Smir calls it the greatest technological rupture in human history, an unparalleled watershed, "the moment the modern world was born." The scale and complexity of industrial organization expanded along with the surge in inventions and knowledge. Although Smir and others acknowledge that this division of time is necessarily arbitrary and temporary—a simplification made to organize scholarly narratives—they still consider the 1880s and 1890s to be the crossing of a threshold.

The First Industrial Revolution was driven by machines: steam power and coal reshaped the economy.

Mechanized manufacturing, agriculture, and transportation reinforced each other. The revolution began in Britain, spread outwards to the European continent, and then across the ocean. Factories not only systematized the production of textiles, chemicals, and new consumer goods, but also amplified the power of capital exponentially. Population growth led to increased wealth. The Second Industrial Revolution was spurred by electricity: electricity, electric lights, and most importantly, electrical communications. Information could be exchanged rapidly over long distances, making standardization, interchangeable parts, and mass production possible. Communications gave rise to the concept of the internet and everything it brought. Businesses expanded and spread, giving birth to the modern corporation. Without the instant conversations enabled by the telephone, large corporations could not possibly employ tens of thousands of people in different locations around the world. Globalization—a modern term with both positive and negative connotations—began here. Historians named the First Industrial Revolution afterward, but poets quickly saw the changes around them and lamented them. William Blake warned of “the dark mills of Satan” and “the shackles of the mind.” Chimneys polluted nature, and machines drained the human spirit. “The world is too entangled with us…/ We keep taking and spending, exhausting our strength,” William Wordsworth complained. In contrast, the changes brought about by electricity were clearly seen at the time and were generally celebrated. They brought wonder and magic. They involved all sorts of gadgets. Thus, those who had just become aware of the machine age quickly recognized and named the Age of Electricity. Parker Benjamin Jr. witnessed Edison's first demonstration of the phonograph in Scientific American, and in 1886 he published a book titled The Age of Electricity with the subtitle From the Spirit of Amber to the Telephone. Benjamin put forward a paradox: we are "surrounded by its wonders," yet these wonders have become familiar on their way to the commonplace. [1] He compared electricity to the genie in Aladdin's lamp, a servant and executor of wishes. It is a spirit hidden within matter, awaiting our command: "If Aladdin's spirit could transport him from one place to another, can't our spirit do the same for us? Much more, for it can transmit our thoughts, even the words we utter, and perhaps one day our faces."

The ever-growing middle class sees itself as a technologically advanced and worldly group. One miracle after another—the telephone, the phonograph, the electric light—created a sense that progress was accelerating, that society was rushing towards an uncertain yet exciting future. Each invention amplified the impact of the previous one.

A visitor to Edison's Menlo Park laboratory saw an "airborne megaphone," designed to shout "from lighthouses, from ships at sea," with a volume equivalent to "two hundred and fifty" people; there were also electric pens for drawing and copying handwriting; electric scissors, electric embroidery machines; and a motion picture projector, through which "one could see phonograph-like sounds moving and speaking." Electricians had harnessed previously unseen forces. The old ways of classifying knowledge were no longer sufficient. The *Scribner Monthly* declared: "These radical new discoveries are particularly noteworthy: they pave the way for new classifications of knowledge, reducing the accumulated vastness of things and all forms of force to a few simple generalizations." What people needed was no less than a new science. Thomas Lockwood, proudly identifying himself as an "electrician for Bell Telephone Company," wrote:

No science has become as prominent as electricity in this age; no other discipline has been so fascinating, so captivating to its followers; when it joins forces with its sister, magnetism, to create modern wonders, no living thing can limit the quantity, nature, and scope of its manifestations.

Thomas Lockwood, who proudly identified himself as an "electrician for Bell Telephone Company," wrote:

No science has become as prominent as electricity in this age; no other discipline has been as fascinating, as captivating to its followers; when it joins forces with its sister, magnetism, to create modern wonders, no living thing can limit the quantity, nature, and scope of its manifestations.

Thomas Lockwood, who proudly identified himself as an "electrician for Bell Telephone Company," wrote:

< ... The most prominent of these manifestations, of course, is the transmission of voice: "This gave rise to a new industry that spread throughout the civilized world in just five years." Its soldiers and missionaries were a growing, technologically savvy generation—not just electricians, but also telephone operators, telephone inspectors, and amateur telephone enthusiasts. Journalists were eager to report on various applications and inventions, some under development, some merely fantasies. They spread slogans and clichés. Electricity is a sleepless sentinel. Electricity has destroyed time and space. The latter part is a timeless formula, repeatedly used by proponents of the telegraph and telephone, inadvertently echoing Alexander Pope's words: "Gods, if only space and time were destroyed, / two lovers could be happy." In an era when people relied on sailboats and steamboats to traverse distances, thousands of miles of ocean meant messages would take weeks to arrive, and everyone still remembered delivering mail on horseback, "eliminating distance" carried weight. Even in the age of railroads and telegraphs, many Americans still believed Lincoln was president weeks after his assassination. Benjamin said that today electricity will illuminate the depths of the ocean and the dark cavities within the human body; it will tear atoms apart and then put them back together. Contemporary chroniclers believed its power was boundless: It could predict impending earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or the barely audible beating of the heart… It could imbue new wine with the flavor of the oldest vintage. It could ring church bells and kitchen chimes… It could speak in our voices hundreds of miles away. Even its most sinister uses couldn't dampen his enthusiasm: “With electric wires that could transmit deadly currents throughout the city, by simply branching off a line to the usual execution site, a condemned could be ended instantly, inevitably, and painlessly with the touch of a button.” Deadly currents? Look at the bright side.

In this electrical age, everything is expanding, growing in scale and importance. The telephone made skyscrapers more feasible than elevators, concentrating commercial life into huge and dense clusters. [2] Everything seemed possible. A frenzy gripped the mass press—"discovery fever." Edison traveled around, giving interviews and preaching. He came up with some futuristic names for his concept, such as "telephone mirror." (One of his technicians found it amusing and retorted with "telescope telephone.") The British satirical magazine Pennywise also caught the fever, and Georges du Maurier drew a cartoon of the telephone mirror: a telephone with a huge screen above the fireplace. “Every evening before bed, Dad and Mom would set up an electric shutter above the fireplace in their bedroom, watching with delight as their children, on their opposite sides, chatted happily with them through the wire.” But that wasn't all; *Clumsy* also delighted readers with illustrations: people floating around in “Edison’s anti-gravity underwear”; it largely blamed this inverted modernity on the inventor: “It soon became clear that if no measures were taken to suppress Mr. Edison, the American inventor, all existing living conditions would be completely changed, and the whole world would be turned upside down.” Adding to the excitement was the approaching milestone on the calendar: 1900—the new century. H. G. Wells published *The Time Machine*, encouraging people to look to the “future.” Mark Twain sent his Connecticut man back to King Arthur’s court, and this unexpected traveler defeated Merlin in magic. The American boasted, “I can put on a little magic trick of mine, which I call the telephone, and he won’t figure it out in a hundred years.” A hundred years ago, the turn of the nineteenth century came and went quietly, causing almost no commotion; but the arrival of the twentieth century brought celebrations, speculations, light festivals, and excited predictions in newspapers across the country.

The Los Angeles Times said on New Year's Day, 1901: "Today we stand on the threshold of the twentieth century. Who dares to predict the progress of the next hundred years?"

In the latter half of the nineteenth century, the tools of civilization grew so rapidly that year after year it was difficult to keep up with the pace of progress. Everything seemed to be in a state of transition. Today's improvement might be obsolete tomorrow... The telephone, the phonograph, the generator, the liquefaction of air, the discovery of bacteriology, and the development of aseptic surgery are just a few of the many extraordinary achievements of the nineteenth century. But these alone were enough to inject new impetus into human endeavors and place civilization on a new foundation.

That optimism, pride, and belief in progress—none of it will emerge unscathed from this new century. Humanity has never been so hopeful about its collective future, but war is looming—and worse—unleashed by technologies that have arrived with a halo.

At this astonishing juncture, civilization displays a new self-awareness, rejoicing in its own existence. Scientific American, speaking of the telephone, wrote: "The invention was complete, and the world was already ready to embrace it." At first it was like a delightful toy; now it is "the fastest-expanding, most complex, and most convenient communication system the world has never seen before." The post office, the printing press, the telegraph—all pale in comparison. The telephone promises "no less than a new organization of society."

This magazine proclaims that anyone, anywhere, no matter how remote, will be able to talk to others, "thus saving countless social and commercial entanglements, unnecessary travel, disappointment, delays, and a whole host of troubles and annoyances—which, under current conditions, make life difficult and unsatisfying." Experts predict that people scattered across the globe will come together—connect with each other—to form a global brain. The telephone will be its nervous system.

[1] Book reviewers in The New York Times welcomed Benjamin's book, considering it a much-needed introductory text at the time, while also taking a jab at the foreign laborers who were building new infrastructure:

“Mr. Benjamin's book is not difficult to understand at all, and we especially recommend The Age of Electricity to those who claim to be well-educated but know nothing about the subject, just like the Italians who are laying underground tunnels for wires in the ditches.”

The Invention of Electricity, The New York Times, October 18, 1886.

[2] John J. Carty, chief engineer of AT&T, later said that “Bell and his successors”—referring to himself—“were the fathers of modern commercial architecture, that is, skyscrapers.” He said to think of how many messages had passed through these buildings and traveled through them; if these messages had to be carried by people, elevators would never have been able to handle such a flow. Quoted from Isil de Sola Poole, ed., The Social Impact of the Telephone (MIT Press, 1977), p. 140. This excerpt is from James Greck, Telephone: A New History, published by Farrar, Strauss and Giroux. Copyright © 2026 James Greck.

data.title: Mankiw's Legal Advice: Can I be considered a fraudster if I help a friend lose money trading cryptocurrency?
data.description:
A friend, unfamiliar with cryptocurrency trading, heard you'd made some money with a few trades and transferred money to you for help. When the market was good, you talked about how much you'd earned; but when the market crashed, the account lost most of its value, and the initial trust began to crumble.

The friend demanded a full refund of the principal. You explained that the money was indeed used to buy cryptocurrencies, but the market was bad, and investment inherently carries risk. However, the friend refused, even threatening, "The money was transferred to you, and now it's lost. If you don't compensate me, I'll call the police and accuse you of fraud." The money is already lost, and the friendship may be over. What's even more worrying is that you were just helping with cryptocurrency trading; how did you suddenly become suspected of fraud?

Whether you need to compensate a friend for losses incurred while helping them trade cryptocurrencies, and whether this constitutes fraud, are two different legal issues. The former depends on the trading relationship between the parties, the actual operations, and the cause of the loss; the latter requires further examination to determine if there was any deception, intent to illegally possess, or other elements constituting a crime.

It's wrong to assume that an operator must compensate for the entire principal simply because they lost money trading cryptocurrency; nor is it wrong to assume that one bears absolutely no responsibility simply because the money did enter the trading platform.

01 If I lost money trading cryptocurrency for a friend, am I obligated to compensate for the principal?

Not necessarily.

After a dispute arises, the most important thing is to define the legal relationship at the time of the initial transfer of money: When your friend transferred the money, was it to ask you to help invest, a loan, or did both parties intend to jointly invest and share the risks?

These legal relationships may all appear to involve "a friend transferring a sum of money," but the rights and obligations are not the same.

If, at the time of the transfer, the recipient issues a promissory note or IOU to gain trust or for any other reason, the legal relationship between the two parties may be considered a loan relationship, and the lender usually has the right to claim the return of the principal according to the loan agreement. If the two parties are indeed entrusting each other with investment, it is necessary to judge based on the agreement on investment arrangements, profit distribution, and risk sharing. If it is just a friend entrusting you to buy and sell virtual currencies on their behalf, then the legal validity of the entrustment relationship and related transactions also involves. In reality, many friends do not sign formal contracts when trading cryptocurrencies on behalf of each other. It might just be a simple message on WeChat, "Can you help me operate this?", followed by a transfer of money. How profits are distributed, who bears the losses, whether contracts are allowed, and whether leverage is permitted are not clearly discussed beforehand. In the event of a dispute, the court often needs to consider chat records, transfer notes, trading accounts, profit settlement, and actual operation details to determine the true transaction arrangements between the two parties. However, there is an easily overlooked issue: even if a brokerage relationship for cryptocurrency trading can be proven, it doesn't automatically mean the brokerage contract is valid. On February 6, 2026, the People's Bank of China and eight other departments issued the "Notice on Further Preventing and Handling Risks Related to Virtual Currencies," reiterating that virtual currencies do not have the same legal status as legal tender, and that conducting virtual currency-related business activities within China constitutes illegal financial activity. The notice also stipulates that any unit or individual investing in virtual currencies and related financial products in violation of public order and good morals will have their related civil legal acts invalid, and any losses arising therefrom shall be borne by the individual. Therefore, in disputes involving entrusted investment in virtual currencies in mainland China, the rules for general legal entrusted financial management cannot be simply applied; the nature of the transaction and the validity of the contract should be examined first, and then the issues of property return and loss liability should be further determined. For investment losses caused solely by market price fluctuations, investors' demands for full compensation of the principal from the broker may not be supported by the court. However, if the agent arbitrarily changes the investment method, conceals the true transaction situation, or does not use the funds as agreed, the legal evaluation may be different. 02 Why did the court rule differently when both cases resulted in losses for helping others trade cryptocurrencies? In judicial practice, different outcomes do exist. In March 2026, a Shandong court announced a dispute over entrusted investment in virtual currency. Liu, through his friend Zhang, entrusted Zhang to purchase a certain virtual currency. Initially, the platform showed daily returns, but soon the platform became unusable, and the relevant person in charge was suspected of criminal offenses. Liu believed that since the money was given to Zhang for investment and could not be recovered, Zhang should return it, so he sued Zhang in court. The court held that the entrusted contract between the two parties regarding the virtual currency investment was invalid. Zhang did not profit from the entrusted transaction; Liu's losses primarily stemmed from the risks associated with participating in related cryptocurrency investment activities. Ultimately, the court rejected Liu's claim for the return of his investment from Zhang. This case illustrates that a friend's assistance in operating an investment and ultimately incurring losses does not necessarily mean that the friend is obligated to bear all the losses. However, another case yielded a different outcome. In June 2026, the Shandong High People's Court published "Lu Fa Case [2026] 281," in which Wang and Zhao were also friends. In 2023, Zhao introduced a cryptocurrency investment project to Wang, and the two discussed prices, profits, and operating methods via WeChat. Subsequently, Wang transferred 72,500 yuan to Zhao, entrusting him to register an account and purchase cryptocurrency. Zhao used the funds to purchase cryptocurrency, but later the platform ceased operations, and Wang was unable to recover his investment, leading him to file a lawsuit. The court ruled the cryptocurrency investment agreement between the two parties invalid, and also held that both parties were at fault for the losses. Wang, knowing the high risks of cryptocurrency investment, still chose to participate and should bear the primary responsibility; Zhao, as the actual operator, knew or should have been aware of the compliance risks of the relevant activities, yet still accepted the entrustment, and also bore some fault. Ultimately, the court determined that investor Wang should bear 80% of the losses, and Zhao, who operated on behalf of Wang, should bear 20%. Both involved friends entrusting each other with cryptocurrency trading, and both involved investment losses, so why were the outcomes different? The key is not whether the two parties are friends, nor simply whether the funds entered the trading platform, but rather how the court determined the validity of the contract, the actual operation, the cause of the loss, and the fault of both parties. This also serves as a reminder to those who trade cryptocurrencies on behalf of others: do not simply assume that as long as the funds were indeed used for investment, losses are necessarily unrelated to you.

Of course, the 80% and 20% figures are merely the allocation of responsibility in the above specific cases, and not the general compensation ratios for disputes involving entrusted cryptocurrency investment. Specific cases should still be judged based on the facts and current laws and policies.

03 ​​My friend reported me to the police for fraud; will the police file a case?

For many people who help friends invest in cryptocurrencies, the biggest worry is not losing money, but rather the other party reporting them to the police. Especially when a friend has clearly stated, "If you don't pay me back, I'll go to the police station and report you for fraud," the person involved inevitably becomes nervous: I only suffered investment losses; will I really be treated as a fraudster?

It needs to be clarified here that reporting to the police is not the same as filing a case, and filing a case does not necessarily mean that a crime has been committed.

According to Article 112 of the Criminal Procedure Law, public security organs shall review reports, accusations, and complaints within their jurisdiction and only file a case when they believe there are criminal facts requiring criminal prosecution. However, determining fraud is not simply about whether the investor suffered losses or whether the operator returned the money. According to Article 266 of the Criminal Law and relevant rules for determining fraud, it is also necessary to examine whether the perpetrator had the intent to illegally possess the funds, and whether they used deceptive means such as fabricating facts or concealing the truth to cause the other party to dispose of property based on a mistaken understanding, thereby causing property loss. For example, if both parties initially agreed to purchase a certain virtual currency, the investor was aware of the associated risks, funds were indeed deposited into the trading account, and there were genuine buying and selling records, but ultimately losses occurred due to a market downturn, then the transaction records, fund flows, and communication between the parties are all important evidence for determining the nature of the event. It's not accurate to conclude that an operator has committed fraud simply based on a final loss or refusal to provide full compensation. Conversely, if someone claims to help a friend buy BTC but never actually invests, instead repeatedly demanding additional funds through fabricated transaction screenshots and fictitious profits, and then uses the funds for personal consumption, debt repayment, or other unauthorized purposes, further investigation is needed to determine if they have the intent to illegally possess the funds or if they have engaged in deceptive behavior. In some cases, even if funds did enter a cryptocurrency trading platform, this doesn't necessarily mean there's no criminal risk. If the perpetrator only uses a small number of real transactions to create the illusion of investment, or knowingly defrauds others of funds by fabricating profits and concealing significant facts despite knowing the project lacks a legitimate basis for operation, and some investment activity did occur, the possibility of fraud cannot be automatically ruled out. Therefore, judging the boundary between ordinary investment disputes and fraud crimes cannot be based solely on whether money was lost in the end; it requires examining the actions taken before and after the funds were transferred. 04. If it's agreed to buy spot, but a contract is secretly opened, will the responsibility differ? Yes. This is a particularly noteworthy situation in cryptocurrency trading disputes. Suppose a friend originally only entrusted you to buy BTC spot, without agreeing to leveraged trading. The operator, however, believes that contract trading is more profitable, so without consent, transfers funds into a contract account and uses a high leverage ratio. Ultimately, the market suddenly fluctuates, the account is forcibly liquidated, and the principal is significantly lost. After the dispute arises, the operator explains, "I also wanted to earn more, but I didn't expect the market to suddenly reverse." Such an explanation may not be sufficient to resolve the responsibility issue. Because spot trading and high-leverage contract trading have significantly different risk structures. Investors' willingness to bear the risk of a decline in cryptocurrency prices does not imply that they have authorized the operator to bear the risk of high-leverage liquidation. Article 929 of the Civil Code stipulates the liability for compensation of the trustee in a valid agency contract, including liability for fault in a paid agency, liability for intentional or gross negligence in a gratuitous agency, and liability for compensation when losses are caused by exceeding authority. However, cryptocurrency investment agency contracts may be invalid, and general agency contract rules cannot be mechanically applied to all cryptocurrency trading cases. The return of property and liability for fault after the relevant contract is invalidated need to be determined in conjunction with Article 157 of the Civil Code and the specific circumstances of the case. But one point cannot be ignored: unauthorized changes to the investment purpose and joint decisions by both parties to participate in high-risk transactions require legal distinction. If an investor explicitly authorizes contract trading, is fully aware of the leverage risks, and continuously monitors account changes, then the determination of liability for negligence differs from when an operator opens a contract without the investor's knowledge. Similarly, if it was originally agreed that only one account would be operated, but the trustee transfers assets to other accounts or wallets without authorization, and cannot explain the reason for the transfer or the destination of the funds, the dispute may further involve the issue of unauthorized disposal of assets. Therefore, those who help friends trade cryptocurrencies should especially not overlook the scope of authorization. Whether both parties agree that contracts can be opened, funds can be transferred, and whether it is permissible to delegate operations to others can all become important facts in the future allocation of liability for negligence. 05 What to do if you've already been asked to pay compensation or even reported to the police? If your friend has already demanded compensation or even stated that they have reported it to the police, the most important thing is not to rush into arguing about who is right and who is wrong, but to quickly clarify the entire transaction process. First, find the original agreement. How did the two parties initially negotiate? Did your friend explicitly request the purchase of a specific cryptocurrency? Were profit sharing, principal protection, or loss mitigation methods agreed upon? Was leverage permitted? This information may be scattered throughout WeChat chats, voice messages, transfer notes, and other communication records. Even without a written contract, you should try to retain the original records completely, avoiding only extracting the parts that are favorable to you. In particular, if there were promises such as "guaranteeing the safety of the principal" or "I will compensate for any losses," these cannot be simply denied after a dispute arises. The legal effect and liability consequences of such statements need to be determined in conjunction with the complete context, the nature of the transaction, and specific legal provisions. Next, match the funds with the transaction records. Where did the money come from? Which account did it go into? When were the purchases and sales made? Were there any withdrawals, transfers, contract transactions, or forced liquidations? All these should be documented and recorded as accurately as possible. For exchange accounts, it's necessary to monitor historical orders, deposit and withdrawal records, asset flows, and contract transaction records. For on-chain assets, you can also verify the flow through wallet addresses and transaction hashes. These materials not only help demonstrate whether funds were actually invested in trading but also verify how the final loss occurred. A single screenshot showing an account loss may not be sufficient to fully prove where the funds went. A decrease in account balance could stem from trading losses, asset transfers, withdrawals, or other operations; a complete record is required for assessment. Finally, decide how to respond based on the progress of the dispute. If the dispute is still in the negotiation stage between friends, first verify the investment amount, existing assets, and actual losses before discussing dispute resolution methods. For unverified amounts, it's unwise to issue IOUs or promise full repayment to avoid creating new legal disputes. If the public security authorities have contacted the parties involved, they should verify the investigating agency and relevant procedures, cooperate with the investigation in accordance with the law, truthfully explain the situation, and seek professional legal assistance in a timely manner. Do not delete chat records, tamper with transaction data, forge contracts, or transfer related assets to evade investigation. In cases involving criminal investigations, complete and accurate fund flows and transaction records are often more valuable evidence than repeated explanations afterward that "I didn't lie to him." Of course, if the investigation reveals that you have indeed engaged in unauthorized disposal, concealment of transactions, or other improper conduct, you cannot simply use "investment is risky" as a reason for exemption from liability. Instead, you should assess the potential civil, administrative, or criminal liabilities based on the specific actions taken. In conclusion, friends helping each other with cryptocurrency trading often initially stems from trust. Some people think they know a little about trading and are willing to help their friends operate their accounts; others see their friends make money and entrust their funds to them, hoping to profit as well. However, cryptocurrency prices fluctuate rapidly. Without clearly defined profit sharing, risk-sharing, and operational authority, losses can easily become a point of contention between the parties. For the actual operators, it's wrong to assume they bear no responsibility simply because they didn't receive management fees or profit from the transaction; similarly, investors shouldn't assume that entrusting money to a friend guarantees a full refund if losses occur. Whether investment losses warrant compensation depends on the transaction relationship, contract validity, actual operations, and the cause of the loss; whether fraud has occurred requires further examination of deceptive behavior, intent to illegally possess, and relevant evidence. Especially when disputes have arisen between the parties, or even when someone has called the police, it is crucial to distinguish between legitimate investment losses, unauthorized operations, unclear asset whereabouts, and fictitious investments. Trust between friends can facilitate an investment, but when a real dispute occurs, what ultimately proves the facts are the initial agreement between the parties and complete transaction evidence.

data.title: The payment CEO who said encryption was useless: Turned around and started building blockchain.
data.description: On November 10th, Alta, a company specializing in building blockchain infrastructure for financial institutions, announced the completion of a $47.5 million Series A funding round, bringing its total funding to $80 million. One of its co-founders is Jack Zhang, CEO of the cross-border payment company Airwallex. In June 2025, he publicly stated that he never understood cryptocurrency and hadn't seen any truly useful applications for it over the past 15 years. Seventeen months later, he became a blockchain builder. This year, he wasn't the only one to turn around. Banks and payment companies that once considered blockchain a scam and an adversary are now integrating it into their underlying systems one after another. Questioning Prices, Betting on Settlement Airwallex's main business is cross-border payments for businesses. It has obtained financial licenses in multiple global markets, connecting local banks and payment networks, enabling businesses to complete payments and exchanges between different currencies. This model has one cost: pre-deposited funds. Taking this model as an example, when a company wants to pay a Brazilian supplier, the payment service provider typically needs to prepare Real funds locally in advance to ensure timely payment. These funds are scattered across different markets and cannot be easily transferred to other regions. The larger the business, the more liquidity buffer needs to be prepared in advance. Alta aims to solve precisely this problem of tied-up funds. Alta estimates that global companies have approximately $4 trillion tied up in these pre-deposited accounts. Launched in June of this year, Alta's first product plans to unlock this "$4 trillion." It aims to allow businesses to replenish funds as needed and allocate temporarily idle funds to tokenized assets to generate returns. Why build your own blockchain? Alta CEO Loong Wang explains that existing blockchains are not designed for the privacy and compliance requirements of global financial institutions, so Alta has directly integrated privacy, programmable compliance, and identity authorization into its chain. Zhang Shuo once questioned whether stablecoins could make payments cheaper; now he's betting on whether blockchain can make funds more efficiently used. Payment giants are vying for a foothold in the underlying infrastructure. Previously, payment companies viewed stablecoins and blockchain as simply payment methods that could be integrated into their systems. Now, they are building their own underlying infrastructure. US payment company Stripe has taken the most comprehensive approach. It completed its acquisition of stablecoin company Bridge in February 2025, and subsequently incubated the payment-specific blockchain Tempo with venture capital firm Paradigm, launching its mainnet in March 2026. Card organizations, on the other hand, are simultaneously acquiring and building their own infrastructure. In March 2026, Mastercard announced its acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure company BVNK for up to $1.8 billion. It is also advancing its Multi-Token Network, providing infrastructure services such as tokenized deposit issuance, transfer, and settlement for banks and financial institutions. Visa's stablecoin settlement pilot program has an annualized scale of approximately $7 billion, with a quarter-on-quarter growth of 50%. It has also joined the Canton Network, a network for institutional finance, becoming a super validator and participating in network operation and governance. Banks are moving settlements onto the blockchain. With payment companies starting to deploy blockchain technology, banks are unlikely to be absent. JPMorgan Chase began developing its blockchain financial infrastructure as early as 2015, launching JPM Coin in 2019 to allow institutional clients to transfer US dollar deposits through the bank's internal permissioned blockchain. In November 2024, JPMorgan Chase renamed its Onyx blockchain business to Kinexys. In November 2025, JPMorgan Chase launched its US dollar deposit token JPMD on Base, becoming the first bank to issue a US dollar deposit token on a public blockchain. As of August 2026, Kinexys' daily trading volume exceeded $7 billion. Swift holds an even more unique position. This global interbank messaging network connects more than 11,000 financial institutions and was once considered a potential replacement for stablecoins. In 2025, Swift announced the construction of a blockchain-based shared ledger to explore enabling banks to conduct 24/7 cross-border payments through tokenized deposits. On July 9, 2026, Swift announced that its blockchain shared ledger was ready for initial use. Seventeen banks, including HSBC, Citibank, Bank of New York Mellon, Wells Fargo, BNP Paribas, and UBS, are preparing to pilot cross-border payments based on tokenized deposits. Putting these cases together, we can see that the scope of competition in the payment industry is expanding. Stablecoins do allow funds to be transferred on the blockchain 24/7, but an on-chain transfer does not equate to a complete cross-border payment. Users still need wallets, transaction gateways, fiat currency deposit and withdrawal channels, foreign exchange liquidity, and service providers that meet the regulatory requirements of different regions. The withdrawal cost issue that Zhang Shuo pointed out years ago still exists. Stablecoins have not automatically eliminated the differences between financial systems in different regions. However, payment companies and banks have begun to try to connect these links. Stripe has merchants and payment gateways and is also building its own payment chain; Visa has a global bank card network and is connecting stablecoins to institutional settlements; JPMorgan Chase hopes to connect bank deposits and on-chain asset markets; Alta is trying to leverage Airwallex's global payment network to enter the corporate fund management and cross-border settlement market. They're not competing for the same product, but rather for different positions in the flow of funds. Payment gateways connect users and merchants, settlement networks handle fund transfers, and banks and financial institutions provide services such as deposits, foreign exchange, custody, and compliance. Whoever can connect these links has a greater chance of becoming a key service provider for on-chain financial activities. This also explains why some traditional financial institutions are starting to build their own blockchains, while others choose to integrate with existing networks. They don't necessarily need to replace public blockchains, nor do they necessarily need to move all transactions to their own chains. Their primary concern is ensuring that the new fund transfer methods don't cause them to lose their original business position. Of course, building a blockchain doesn't equate to controlling the market. Whether Alta can truly reduce the cost of pre-deposited funds for businesses, whether Tempo can attract enough payment applications, whether Visa's stablecoin settlement can expand to more institutions, and whether banks' on-chain deposits can form a large-scale business all still need time to verify. However, one thing is clear: when stablecoins begin to enter the payment and financial system, the competition will no longer be just about issuing a digital dollar, but about who can provide payment, settlement, and fund management services for these funds. Zhang Shuo once believed that stablecoins could not solve the cost problem of cross-border payments. Now, Alta, which he co-founded, is attempting to find new answers in the fund management and settlement processes. Whether stablecoins can ultimately transform cross-border payments remains to be seen. However, payment companies and banks are no longer content to remain mere bystanders in this transformation.
